tagline: Inca stone, desert coast, Amazon green
overview:
Peru occupies the western side of South America, facing the Pacific Ocean and bordering Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia and Chile. At about 1.29 million km² it is the third-largest country in South America, roughly twice the size of Texas, and it packs three completely different worlds into one map: a bone-dry coastal desert, the high Andes, and the Amazon rainforest.

About 34 million people live in Peru. Spanish is the main language, and Quechua and Aymara, spoken in the highlands since before the Spanish arrived, are official too. Lima, the capital, is a huge coastal city where it almost never rains, home to nearly a third of all Peruvians.

Peru is a presidential republic. It is famous for Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel perched on a green ridge, for potatoes in thousands of varieties, and for a food scene that has made Lima one of the world's great eating cities.
landAndNature: The Andes run the length of Peru, with more than thirty peaks above 6,000 meters, including Huascarán at 6,768 meters. Between the ranges sit high plateaus and Lake Titicaca, the world's highest large navigable lake, shared with Bolivia. East of the mountains, rivers gather into the Amazon, and rainforest covers more than half the country. The coast is desert because the cold Humboldt Current chills the sea air; that same current makes Peru's waters some of the richest fishing grounds on the planet. Vicuñas, whose wool is the finest in the world, graze the altiplano, condors ride mountain updrafts, and the rainforest holds pink river dolphins, jaguars and giant otters.
peopleAndCulture: Peruvian food blends Indigenous ingredients with Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese cooking. Ceviche, raw fish cured in lime juice with chili and onion, is the national dish; lomo saltado is a stir-fry that came from Chinese immigrant kitchens. Farmers grow thousands of potato varieties and grains like quinoa at altitudes where little else survives. Andean music uses the panpipe and the small stringed charango, and weavers make textiles in patterns handed down for centuries. Festivals mix Catholic saints with older beliefs, as at Inti Raymi in Cusco, a re-enacted Inca sun festival each June. Soccer is the biggest sport, and paleta frontón and surfing are popular on the coast.
history: Peru holds some of the oldest cities in the Americas; Caral on the coast dates back about 5,000 years. The Moche, Nazca, Wari and Chimú cultures followed, leaving pyramids, gold work and the Nazca Lines. From the 1400s the Inca built the largest empire in the Americas, running from Ecuador to Chile, linked by 40,000 kilometers of stone roads and governed from Cusco without wheels, iron or writing as Europeans knew it. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and a small Spanish force captured the emperor Atahualpa, and within years the empire fell, with disease killing far more people than fighting did. Spain ruled for nearly 300 years, mining silver at Potosí with forced Indigenous labor. Peru declared independence in 1821. An internal conflict with the Shining Path guerrillas in the 1980s and 1990s killed tens of thousands.
funFacts: Peru grows more than 3,000 varieties of potato, in colors from purple to yellow and shapes from knobby to smooth.
The Nazca Lines are huge figures of a hummingbird, monkey and spider scratched into the desert, best seen from the air.
Inca builders fitted giant stones together so precisely that a knife blade cannot slip between them, without any mortar.
Machu Picchu was never found by the Spanish, and the outside world learned of it only in 1911.
The Inca recorded numbers and possibly words using quipus, bundles of knotted strings that scholars are still decoding.
